analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to affirmatively approve every major federal regulation before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a markup, or any vote; it had 1 sponsor and 7 Republican cosponsors in the Senate.
analysis.plain_summary: Under this bill, any federal agency rule with an economic effect of $100 million or more would have no force unless both chambers of Congress passed a law approving it within 70 legislative days — if they did not, the rule would die by default. It would also treat major agency guidance documents as rules requiring approval, put a 10-year expiration date on all major rules, bar agencies from issuing a costly new rule unless they offset it by repealing an old one, and give companies a legal defense and a right to sue against rules. Supporters said it would force Congress to own the laws it delegates; opponents of the approach note it would make most significant new protections disappear whenever one chamber declines to act.
analysis.who_benefits: Large regulated firms — in energy, manufacturing, finance, pharmaceuticals, mining, and other industries — whose conduct is constrained by major federal rules. Because approval would be the exception and inaction the default, any major rule a reluctant or divided Congress failed to approve within 70 legislative days would simply never take effect, and existing major rules would expire after 10 years unless Congress re-upped them. Companies would also gain an affirmative defense in enforcement cases and a private right of action to challenge rules.

how_it_helps.text: Any major rule — one costing the economy $100 million or more — would take effect only if Congress enacted a joint resolution approving it within 70 session or legislative days; otherwise the rule would be deemed not approved and would not take effect [S2].

The bill creates an annual 'regulatory budget': a significant regulatory action would have no effect unless the agency offset its cost by issuing a deregulatory action, or the OMB Director approved it in writing in advance [S2].

Each major rule would cease to have effect 10 years after approval unless Congress enacted a new joint resolution extending it, and agencies could not reissue substantially the same rule without new statutory authority [S2].

Defendants in federal enforcement proceedings would gain an affirmative defense if a person of ordinary intelligence could not have anticipated from the statute's wording that their conduct was unlawful, and any person could sue to block an agency's failure to follow the new process or to challenge an agency's decision that a rule is not 'major' [S2].

Significant guidance documents — non-binding agency interpretations with large economic effects — would be treated as rules requiring congressional approval, and all guidance documents would have to be published online in a single location [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Everyone who depends on federal regulation: workers, consumers, and communities who rely on clean air and water, workplace safety, safe food and drugs, and fair financial markets. The people who would bear the cost are those exposed to hazards when protections die by default — including when one chamber simply declines to schedule a vote. Supporters counter that the current system lets unelected agencies impose the costs, and that Congress should bear the accountability.

drawbacks.text: Under the bill, inaction kills: a major rule dies unless both chambers pass and the President signs an approval within 70 legislative days, so in any period of divided government or crowded calendar most significant new protections — and the updates agencies use to respond to new hazards — would never take effect [S2].

The bill would subject even significant guidance documents to the approval process, requiring Congress to legislate on thousands of routine technical and interpretive agency statements, a volume of work Congress has never shown it can handle [S2].
The affirmative defense and the deregulatory 'offset' requirement would weaken enforcement and create a one-way ratchet in which agencies could add protections only by repealing others [S2].

Defenders of the current system argue that Congress already wrote the statutes agencies implement and can overturn any rule through the existing Congressional Review Act, so replacing agency expertise with hundreds of mandatory approval votes would substitute delay and political bargaining for protection [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — making Congress accountable for the rules made under the laws it passes — is a real constitutional argument, and the transparency provisions (online publication of guidance, GAO studies of rule costs) are unobjectionable. But the design goes far beyond accountability: the default is death of the rule rather than a vote, approval must clear both chambers and the President within 70 days, all major rules would expire after 10 years, and new rules would need deregulatory offsets. In practice, the businesses regulated by major rules would gain far more than the public would, since most approvals would never happen while the costs of unchecked hazards fall on workers, consumers, and communities. The bill is poorly designed even for people who share its goal, because the guidance-document mandate and the 70-day clock would grind large parts of government to a halt.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee the day it was introduced; the committee never took it up, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Rand Paul introduced the bill in the Senate on September 18, 2024, with six Republican original cosponsors [S1].
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs [S4].
No further action appears in the record: no hearing, no markup, no committee report, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1].
The bill's text would have required a joint resolution of approval, signed into law within 70 legislative days, for any major federal rule to take effect [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without any action, the people better off are workers, consumers, and communities who rely on federal protections that would have needed an affirmative act of Congress to survive; regulated industries gained nothing from the outcome.

sides.party_line_note: All 8 sponsors and cosponsors were Senate Republicans (7 of 49); no Democrat supported the bill, and the Democratic-led committee never acted on it.

industries.industry: Broadly regulated industries — energy, manufacturing, finance, pharmaceuticals, mining
industries.note: Every major rule costing $100 million or more would die unless both chambers passed and the President signed an approval within 70 legislative days, so the rules these firms face would default to nonexistent. The savings would come at the cost of the air, water, workplace, and financial protections the public relies on [S2].

Agencies would lose the ability to put most significant rules or major guidance into effect on their own authority, and would face a deregulatory-offset requirement that caps new protections [S2]. The bill also exempts Federal Reserve monetary policy rules, deregulatory actions, and hunting, fishing, and camping rules from the approval process [S2].
The bill adds an affirmative defense — violators escape liability if the underlying statute was not clear enough — and a private right of action to sue agencies and invalidate rules [S2].
